explainedBy: Steve at the plateau, slumped over the notes of his old digit groupings, has to give up the method that had always worked.

storyboard.claim: Steve had to abandon the strategy that felt safe and had worked; comfort is where improvement stops.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve slumped and worried, holding the notes of his old grouping method in the lab room.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the plateau story from the previous beats.
storyboard.addedInformation: The worried slump over his own notes shows the old method failing him.

explainedBy: Result of the rebuild: the same Steve, now celebrating beside his running-time stopwatch trick, reached 83 digits because he left the comfortable strategy.

storyboard.claim: Had he stayed comfortable with his 22-digit strategy, he would never have reached 83.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same lab stage: Steve goes from slumped to celebrating, the stopwatch of his running-time trick beside him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; the slump turns into celebration (plateau -> breakthrough).
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the counterfactual "never" is carried by the narration; the picture shows the result he did reach.

explainedBy: The host recaps the cases so far: the Tokyo music school (piano keyboard) and the psychology lab.

storyboard.claim: We have seen focused adaptation in a Tokyo music school and a Pennsylvania psychology lab.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host speaking beside the piano keyboard of the Tokyo study.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: A recap and a turn away from the lab.
storyboard.addedInformation: The keyboard recalls the perfect-pitch study the viewer already saw.

explainedBy: Everyday life raises the question: if the brain is this plastic, why do ordinary people not improve?

storyboard.claim: Step out of the lab and look at the everyday things people do.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The everyman walking down a street: normal life.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the lab cases to everyday life.
storyboard.addedInformation: The ordinary man on a street shows the move from lab to daily life.

callout.text: why are we not world class?

explainedBy: The question: if the brain is this plastic, why does the ordinary person stay ordinary at daily tasks?

storyboard.claim: If the brain is so plastic, why don't we become world class at daily tasks just by living?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same street: the everyman stops walking and slumps, worried, the brain icon beside him.
storyboard.onScreenText: world class at our daily tasks
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same man and street; he stops and the brain appears with the question.
storyboard.addedInformation: The brain icon names the plastic organ the question is about.

explainedBy: Start of the tennis story: an everyday player walks onto the court on a sunny weekend, racket beside him.

storyboard.claim: Picture an everyday tennis player on a gorgeous sunny weekend.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The everyman, happy, walking outdoors with the tennis racket icon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: A new example: the weekend tennis player.
storyboard.addedInformation: The racket says who he is: a recreational tennis player.

explainedBy: The player hits balls and plays doubles for fun; his skills got automated after a few early lessons.

storyboard.claim: He hits balls against a wall, plays doubles with friends, has a great time; early lessons automated his backhand.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same court: the player now celebrating, racket beside him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; walking turns into playing and enjoying.
storyboard.addedInformation: The celebrate pose shows the fun, relaxed state of his play.

explainedBy: Result: twenty years of the same relaxed play leave him exactly where he was; the joy fades into a blank stand-still.
noVisual: "20 years pass" and "no better" have no visual form beyond the frozen, unchanged player; the callout carries the number.

storyboard.claim: Twenty years pass in this relaxed state, and doing something for 20 years makes you no better at it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same court: the same player, now standing still with a blank face beside the racket.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; celebration drops to a blank stand-still.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the time passing is carried by the callout; the blank face shows no progress.

explainedBy: The mechanism of naive practice: the moment a skill becomes automatic, progression stops.

storyboard.claim: This is naive practice: once a skill becomes automatic and the basal ganglia takes over, progress ends.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow: becomes automatic -> progression stops.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the tennis story to the mechanism behind it.
storyboard.addedInformation: The flow states cause and effect directly.

explainedBy: The same mechanism carried to its end: once progress stops you are locked in at that level.

storyboard.claim: Your progression is over; you are permanently locked in at that level of competence.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same flow gains a third step: locked in.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same flow; one more label (locked in).
storyboard.addedInformation: Adds the permanent result to the chain.

explainedBy: Why it happens: the brain wants to save energy, so it automates the swing and then stops building new circuits.

storyboard.claim: The brain saves energy: automaticity is cheap, so it automates the swing and stops building circuits.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow: save energy -> automate the swing -> no new circuits.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The cause behind the previous chain: the brain's energy saving.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the brain's motive as the first link of the chain.

explainedBy: The assumption that time served (the clock) equals mastery, about to be tested on Franklin.
noVisual: An assumption being rejected has no object; the struck callout carries it while Franklin enters as the example.

storyboard.claim: We assume time served equals mastery gained; look at Benjamin Franklin.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Old Franklin in his parlor; the assumption struck through.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the brain mechanism to a historical counter-example.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: Franklin is introduced; the rejection lives in the struck text.

explainedBy: Franklin, the genius, sits down at the chessboard he was obsessed with.

storyboard.claim: Franklin was a polymath genius, but consider his obsession with chess.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same parlor: Franklin now sitting, the chessboard in front of him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same Franklin; he sits down and the chessboard appears.
storyboard.addedInformation: The chessboard names the activity the story is about.

explainedBy: Franklin keeps playing chess for fifty years, from evening until sunrise.
noVisual: "50 years" and "6 p.m. until sunrise" are durations; only the callout can state them.

storyboard.claim: He played chess for 50 years, from 6 p.m. until sunrise, obsessed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same stage: Franklin at the chessboard; the callout gives the span.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; the callout adds the 50 years.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the duration is text-carried; the picture keeps him at the board.

explainedBy: Despite fifty years and games against Europe's best, Franklin at the chessboard stays average: his smile drops.

storyboard.claim: He even played Europe's grandmasters as a diplomat in France, but his skill stayed stubbornly average.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same stage: Franklin's face turns sad at the board.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; his face falls (effort -> no progress).
storyboard.addedInformation: The sad face at the same board shows the result of decades of play.

explainedBy: Why: Franklin just plays on, smiling at the board, never studying his losses or drilling his weaknesses.

storyboard.claim: He just played; he never analyzed his losses or drilled his weaknesses.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same stage: Franklin back to a carefree smile at the board, no notes, no study.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; the cause is given: he just played.
storyboard.addedInformation: The carefree face with nothing but the board shows play without study.

explainedBy: Franklin never replays a bad move; he simply enjoys the game and plays for fun.

storyboard.claim: He never paused to replay a bad move ten times; he just played for fun.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same stage: Franklin delighted, celebrating a game at the chessboard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; sitting turns into celebrating.
storyboard.addedInformation: The celebrate pose makes "for fun" visible.

explainedBy: The verdict on Franklin: this is naive practice, a harmless trap when the stakes are only weekend chess.

storyboard.claim: He was trapped by naive practice, which is relatively harmless for weekend chess or campfire guitar.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same stage: Franklin at ease beside the board, a wry smile.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; the story closes with the verdict.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the "harmless" verdict is mostly text-carried.

explainedBy: The same trap moved into medicine, where it becomes frightening: an ordinary person afraid in a hospital.

storyboard.claim: Applied to high-stakes professions, naive practice has terrifying implications.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The everyman, afraid, in a hospital with the medical icon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From weekend chess to medicine.
storyboard.addedInformation: The medical icon names the high-stakes field; the afraid face gives the stakes.

explainedBy: The comparison we make: the confident veteran doctor with 20 years versus the nervous young resident just out of med school.

storyboard.claim: For major surgery I want the doctor with 20 years, not the one 2 years out of med school.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The grey veteran doctor, confident and talking, next to a nervous young resident.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the two doctors being compared.
storyboard.addedInformation: The age and confidence contrast shows who we intuitively trust.

explainedBy: We reward repetition: the veteran doctor holds the money we pay senior surgeons, the resident beside him has none.

storyboard.claim: We trust that repetition equals mastery; that is why we pay senior surgeons more.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same two doctors; the veteran now holds a coin.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same pair; the veteran now holds the reward.
storyboard.addedInformation: The coin in the veteran's hand shows the higher pay.

explainedBy: The data flips the intuition: the 20-year veteran slumps as the worse diagnostician, the young resident is the better one.

storyboard.claim: Research shows doctors with 20 years are often objectively worse than those 2-3 years out of school.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same pair: the veteran's confidence drops to a sad slump, the resident brightens.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same pair; their faces swap (trusted -> worse, nervous -> better).
storyboard.addedInformation: The swapped faces show the reversal the data reveals.

explainedBy: Why the veteran is worse: he has automated his daily routine and works with a blank, absent face.

storyboard.claim: How is it possible? The older doctors have completely automated their daily routines.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same pair: the veteran now stands blank and absent.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same pair; the veteran's face goes blank (the cause).
storyboard.addedInformation: The blank face shows routine without thought.

explainedBy: The veteran's mechanism: same cases and same treatments put the brain on energy-saving autopilot.

storyboard.claim: They see the same cases, prescribe the same treatments, and their brains shift into autopilot.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow: same cases -> same treatments -> autopilot.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The mechanism behind the blank veteran.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows repetition leading to autopilot as a chain.

explainedBy: The contrast: the young resident, worried, bent over her notes, sweating every detail.

storyboard.claim: The veterans lose their sharp edge; the new doctors are sweating every detail.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young resident, worried, holding her notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the veterans' autopilot to the residents' effort.
storyboard.addedInformation: The notes and worried face show active, careful work.

explainedBy: The resident actively checks: she picks up the reference book on "checking references".

storyboard.claim: They have no autopilot yet: they agonize over diagnostic steps, check references, challenge assumptions.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same resident; she reaches for and takes a reference book.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same resident; notes give way to a reference book she picks up.
storyboard.addedInformation: The deed of taking the book shows the checking.

explainedBy: Her effort puts her at the edge of her ability: the resident with her book beside the ledge.

storyboard.claim: They operate closer to the uncomfortable edge of learning.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same resident holding the book; a ledge appears beside her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same resident; the ledge adds where she is working.
storyboard.addedInformation: The ledge places her effort at the edge of ability.

explainedBy: The veteran on autopilot: his skills do not just plateau, they decline; he slumps alone.

storyboard.claim: On autopilot, the veterans' skills gradually decline; automation is the enemy of mastery.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The veteran doctor alone, slumping sadly.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Back to the veteran: his result.
storyboard.addedInformation: The slump shows the decline.

explainedBy: The general rule: once the brain does a task without effort, it stops growing; the everyman stands blank beside the brain.

storyboard.claim: The second your brain can do surgery, drive, or hit a backhand without effort, it stops growing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The everyman with a blank face beside the brain icon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the doctors to everyone.
storyboard.addedInformation: The brain icon names what stops growing.

explainedBy: The conclusion: to improve we must outwit the brain's urge to automate; the everyman now points at the brain.

storyboard.claim: Comfort is where improvement stops; to get better we must circumvent the brain's desire to automate.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same stage: the everyman wakes from blank and points at the brain.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; blank -> pointing at the brain (the target to outwit).
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the pointing gives the turn to action; the rule is text-carried.

explainedBy: The way into deliberate practice: an everyday music lesson.
noVisual: Announcing an upcoming definition has no event to show; the host frames it.

storyboard.claim: We must define the rigorous alternative; first, a music lesson shows what does not work.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host speaking in a music classroom.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the problem to the search for a solution.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: text-carried transition.

explainedBy: The scene: a frustrated teacher stares at a young student with a trumpet.

storyboard.claim: A frustrated music teacher stares at a young student holding a trumpet.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The worried teacher facing the boy, the trumpet between them.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: A new scene: the music lesson.
storyboard.addedInformation: The trumpet and the teacher-student pair set the lesson.

explainedBy: The teacher questions the boy: how many times did you play it, and how many times correctly?

storyboard.claim: The teacher asks how many times he played it (10 or 20) and how many times correctly.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same pair: the teacher now pointing at the boy, questioning him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same pair; the teacher starts asking.
storyboard.addedInformation: The teacher addressing the boy shows the questioning.

explainedBy: The boy answers with a blank stare ("I just played it"), and the teacher sags.

storyboard.claim: The kid stares blankly: "Don't know. I just played it."
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same pair: the boy's face goes blank, the teacher slumps.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same pair; the question meets a blank answer.
storyboard.addedInformation: The blank boy and the slumping teacher show the failed answer.

explainedBy: "I just played it" is named: the anthem of naive practice; trying hard is not enough.
noVisual: Naming the pattern adds no new event; the kept scene and the callout carry it.

storyboard.claim: "I just played it" is the anthem of naive practice; trying hard is not enough.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same lesson held; the label names it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same scene; the callout names what we saw.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: label only, the scene is unchanged.

explainedBy: The ladder of practice: putting in hours (naive) and purposeful practice are only stepping stones.

storyboard.claim: Hours are not enough; even purposeful practice is only a stepping stone.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow: naive practice -> purposeful practice.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the lesson to the levels of practice.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows purposeful practice as a step beyond naive practice, not the end.

explainedBy: The top of the ladder: deliberate practice is the gold standard, with four strict elements.

storyboard.claim: The gold standard, the only thing that reliably creates world-class experts, is deliberate practice.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same flow gains its last step: deliberate practice.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same flow; one more label (deliberate practice).
storyboard.addedInformation: Completes the progression with the gold standard.
